_note: 'says' is what the NMC document states, in plain language. 'interp' (optional) is Digilantern's interpretation or recommended practice and is always shown with an 'Our interpretation' label. Every rule needs at least one clause ID that exists in clauses.json.

themes.title: Who and what is covered
themes.intro: Who must follow these rules, and who is still responsible when an agency does the work.

themes.title: What counts as advertising
themes.intro: The definition is wide. Information that is not promotional is exempt.

themes.title: Showing who the doctor is
themes.intro: Electronic posts must carry doctor identity and registration details.

themes.title: Claims, superlatives and results
themes.intro: The most common risk in our work: words like “best”, “guaranteed” and “10,000+ patients”.

themes.title: Patients: stories, photos and privacy
themes.intro: Testimonials and before-and-after content are barred. Consent does not fix them.

themes.title: Reviews, ratings and fake engagement
themes.intro: Do not ask for, buy, share or fake reviews and engagement.

themes.title: AI-generated content
themes.intro: AI promotional content is restricted. What is allowed must be labelled.

themes.title: Offers, fees and how agencies are paid
themes.intro: Inducement-style offers and lead-linked payments are restricted.

themes.title: Endorsements and third parties
themes.intro: No celebrity, influencer, patient or employee promotion, and no workarounds.

themes.title: What is still allowed
themes.intro: Education, announcements, talks and factual clinic information.

themes.title: Clinic and hospital rules; doctor photos
themes.intro: What a clinic may say about itself.

themes.intro: What happens to the doctor or clinic if the rules are broken.

rules.says: The Guidelines come into force with immediate effect (cover notice). The Guidelines themselves say they come into force on the date NMC publishes them.
rules.interp: The document gives no transition period and does not say what happens to content already live. We treat live content as in scope from 06/10/2026.

rules.says: The Guidelines apply to Registered Medical Practitioners (doctors on the National or a State register) and to hospitals and clinical establishments.
rules.interp: Our clients are doctors and clinics, so everything we publish in their name is in scope. Wellness or diagnostics clients that are not clinical establishments need a scope check with legal counsel.

rules.says: Using an agency, platform, influencer or other intermediary does not by itself free the doctor or institution from responsibility for content they authorised, commissioned, sponsored, adopted or knowingly permitted.
rules.interp: The document puts responsibility on the doctor or institution, not on us. Our commercial risk is client loss and contract disputes. That is why every change needs written client approval.

rules.says: If the Guidelines clash irreconcilably with the NMC Act or the 2002 Regulations, those prevail. For hospitals, the Clinical Establishments Act or Rules or State Act prevail.
rules.interp: State rules can be stricter. Ask each client which State Act and State Medical Council apply.

rules.says: NMC may issue clarifications, advisories, SOPs or procedural instructions later.
rules.interp: Someone in Leadership should own a monthly check of NMC announcements and update this guide.

rules.says: “Advertisement” means any communication in any medium that directly or indirectly solicits or promotes a doctor's or hospital's services, reputation, skills, qualifications, achievements, facilities or commercial healthcare services.

Digital, social-media, sponsored, targeted, influencer-led, search-engine, platform-based, audio-visual and AI-generated promotional communication is treated as advertising where its content or the way it is spread is promotional.
rules.interp: SEO pages, Google Business Profile posts and reels all count if they are promotional in content or in how they are pushed.

rules.says: “Medium of advertisement” includes, but is not limited to, print, TV, radio, social media, websites and blogs, messaging apps (WhatsApp, Telegram, Facebook), podcasts, influencer marketing, digital campaigns, sponsored posts, AI-generated promotion, public interviews, news articles intended for promotion, online healthcare platforms, and any audio-visual or digital communication.
Sharing information with the public in the normal course, without being promotional and without any intent for commercial benefit, is exempt from the definition of advertisement.
rules.interp: This is why we do not blanket-delete educational content. Test each piece: does it push the clinic, ask for bookings, make claims, or give the doctor a promotional portrayal? If not, it can stay. If so, rewrite.

rules.says: Information about the availability or installation of equipment, technology, diagnostic facilities or services may be shared as fact, as long as it has no claims of superiority, guaranteed accuracy, guaranteed outcomes, comparison or other misleading or unverifiable representation.
rules.interp: “We have [device name] installed” is fine. “Most advanced”, “most accurate” or “painless with our laser” is not.

rules.says: A doctor publishing electronic media posts must transparently disclose their name, qualifications, registration status and SMR/NMR registration number.
rules.interp: The document does not say where on a page or post. Our working practice: show it on the doctor profile, in the site footer, and in the byline of every blog post. On social, put it in the bio and in the caption where the doctor appears. Confirm with legal counsel.

rules.says: A clinical establishment publishing electronic media posts must transparently disclose the names of its doctors with qualifications, registration status and SMR/NMR registration number.
rules.interp: We collect this for every doctor at onboarding. Landing pages and ad destinations also carry it.

rules.says: A hospital website directory of its doctors (names, recognised qualifications, specialties, registration details, availability) that serves a patient-information function is regarded as materially distinct from a paid or promotional advertisement.
rules.interp: A plain factual team directory is the safest format for doctor information.

rules.says: A doctor must not advertise “Guaranteed cures”, “Best doctors”, “No.1 Specialist”, “100% success”, “painless treatment”, “Miracle treatment”, “Exclusive cure” or any other unverifiable or exaggerated claim.
A doctor must not advertise personal achievements, professional success rates or the number of patients treated, with illustrative assertions.
rules.interp: We read counters such as “10,000+ patients treated” and “98% satisfied” as covered. “Years of experience” is not named in the document, so it goes to the grey-areas page.

rules.says: No doctor or hospital may make comparative claims such as “best”, “No.1”, “leading”, “most trusted”, “top”, “number one”, “unmatched” or similar, unless the claim is objectively verifiable, based on a transparent and independently ascertainable methodology, and otherwise lawful.
rules.interp: Treat these words as banned by default. Only a client who can show an independent, published methodology can keep one, and Leadership signs off.

rules.says: Any ranking or award used in advertising must be capable of independent verification. Material conditions, methodology, relevant date and details of the awarding organisation or firm must be disclosed where needed to avoid misleading the public.
rules.interp: Before any award badge is used, collect the awarding body, date and methodology. If it is a pay-to-feature or nomination-fee award, treat it as unverifiable.

rules.says: A doctor must not publish statements that create unrealistic expectations, misrepresent outcomes, conceal risks, promote unproven therapies or secret remedies, or promote treatments whose composition, scientific basis, safety or efficacy is not adequately established.
rules.interp: Phrases such as “permanent results”, “no side effects” and “risk-free” create expectations or hide risks. Rewrite them with balanced, evidence-based wording.

rules.says: A doctor must not run advertisements or activities meant to create unnecessary demand for procedures, promote unnecessary diagnostics, or promote fear-based marketing.
rules.interp: Hooks like “Ignore this and lose your hair forever” are fear-based. Education should inform, not alarm.

rules.says: Hospital communication must not contain guarantees of cure or outcome, unverifiable or exaggerated claims, comparative superiority, patient solicitation or inducement, or promotional portrayal of an individual doctor. The form, medium or frequency must not turn factual information into solicitation or self-aggrandisement.
rules.interp: Frequency matters. Daily promotional posting or heavy retargeting of the same factual information could be read as solicitation. Confirm with legal counsel.

rules.says: Hoardings and billboards in public space may be used only to share factual information on infrastructure and facilities. Unverified or unverifiable claims are treated as for commercial gain and are prohibited.

A doctor must not publish cases for promotion, advertise surgical results, display “before and after” photographs, publicise celebrity patients or promote personal success stories. The only stated exception is publication strictly for scientific or educational purposes with anonymised patient consent.
rules.interp: We treat the exception as narrow: a genuine scientific or educational case, anonymised, with documented consent, not placed on a service page or a campaign. Any use goes to Leadership and legal counsel first.

rules.says: Patient information, photographs, videos, medical records, clinical images, treatment details, testimonials or other identifiable information must not be used for advertising unless the law permits it and the necessary consent and safeguards are in place.

Patient consent does not by itself make a testimonial, endorsement, promotional patient story, before-and-after depiction, success claim or other practice permissible if these Guidelines or the law otherwise prohibit it.
rules.interp: A signed consent form is not a reason to keep a testimonial or before-and-after on a site or ad.

rules.says: Where consent is legally required it must be specific, informed, voluntary, documented and capable of verification, and must follow privacy and data-protection law.

Even where disclosure is lawful, reasonable safeguards must be taken: avoid unnecessary disclosure of names, and crop, blur or black out birth marks, identification marks or other identifying details.
Doctors and clinics must not share patient data, such as names, faces or anomalies, that can be identified publicly.
rules.interp: This covers clinic reels with patients in frame, review replies that mention a treatment, and screenshots of chats.

rules.says: Advertising that involves processing, publishing, storing, disclosing or otherwise using digital personal data must comply, to the extent applicable, with the IT Act 2000 and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 and Rules made in 2025.
rules.interp: Lead forms, remarketing audiences, WhatsApp and email lists all use personal data. Get a data-protection review with legal counsel.

rules.says: Live broadcast or commercial dissemination of surgical or clinical procedures must follow the applicable NMC framework on live surgery, covering patient safety, consent, privacy, educational purpose, sponsorship, commercialisation and professional conduct.
rules.interp: The notice points to a separate NMC framework that we do not have. Do not film or stream procedures for marketing until we have it.

rules.says: No doctor or hospital may solicit, purchase, procure, manipulate or cause to be published fake, paid or misleading patient reviews, ratings, testimonials, endorsements or recommendations for promoting medical services.
rules.interp: We read “solicit” as including review-request campaigns, QR codes, WhatsApp requests, incentives and review gating. Whether a neutral “leave feedback” link is allowed is unclear (see grey areas).

rules.says: A doctor shall not request or share patient testimonials, recommendations, endorsements or reviews for professional promotion on social media.
rules.interp: No resharing reviews, screenshots, review stories or “patient love” posts.

rules.says: No doctor or hospital may procure, manipulate or cause a third party to procure or manipulate fake followers, likes, reviews, ratings, testimonials, comments, views or other digital engagement, or manipulate search rankings, visibility or algorithms to create a misleading impression of professional standing.
rules.interp: We do not buy followers, engagement pods, fake reviews or link schemes. The document does not define what counts as “manipulating” search rankings, so normal SEO needs to stay clearly white-hat.

rules.says: Healthcare platforms hosting doctors must follow NMC ethical advertising norms, must not rank doctors for payment, and must keep listing practices transparent.
rules.interp: Paid “featured” or “top-ranked” placement on directory listings is a risk for the client.

rules.says: An AI-generated promotional campaign for commercial interest is prohibited. AI-generated promotional content that otherwise conforms must carry a source mark explicitly stating that it is AI-generated.
rules.interp: The first sentence and the second sentence pull in different directions, and the document does not explain how. Until clarified, we treat fully AI-generated promotional content as high risk and label anything AI-generated that is used. See grey areas.

rules.says: AI-generated or AI-assisted content must not be used to create or spread misleading, deceptive or unverifiable representations about diagnosis, treatment, clinical outcomes, professional qualifications, patient experiences or healthcare services.
rules.interp: AI-written medical copy needs a doctor's fact-check before publishing.

rules.says: AI must not be used to create or manipulate a patient's image, testimonial, voice or clinical outcome, or to create a synthetic endorsement or representation purporting to be of an actual patient, doctor or other person.
rules.interp: No AI avatars of doctors, AI voice-overs in the doctor's voice, AI-generated “patients”, or AI-retouched results.

rules.says: Where AI-generated or materially AI-altered content is used in a way that its artificial nature may reasonably matter to the audience's understanding, appropriate disclosure must be made.
Patient information used as input to an AI system must comply with privacy, confidentiality, data-protection and professional-ethics requirements.
rules.interp: Never paste patient details, photos or chat logs into AI tools.

rules.says: No doctor or hospital may use discounts, limited-period offers, contests, coupons, gifts, cashbacks, referral benefits, free procedures or similar inducements in a way likely to encourage unnecessary consultation, diagnostic investigation or treatment, or that otherwise amounts to solicitation of patients.
rules.interp: The test in the text is “likely to encourage unnecessary” care or “solicitation”. We take the cautious view: no festival offers, limited-time deals, giveaways, referral rewards or free-procedure promotions.

rules.says: Any lawful disclosure of charges, packages or fees must be factual, transparent and not misleading.
A doctor may make a public declaration of consultation fees.

No doctor may offer, pay, solicit, receive or take part in any commission, rebate, bonus, gift, gratuity, referral fee, lead-generation fee or other consideration for promotion or advertisement where it is connected with referral, recommendation or procurement of patients, specimens or materials.
rules.interp: Applies to the client's dealings with anyone, including agencies and aggregators. Whether our performance-linked fees fall inside this is a Leadership and legal question.

rules.says: Engagement of advertising agencies, digital marketing agencies, influencers or online platforms must not be structured so that payment or consideration is linked to the procurement or referral of individual patients.
rules.interp: Our fee structures need a review. Payment per patient, per booked appointment or per lead may be affected. The document does not say whether a “lead” counts as procuring an individual patient. See grey areas.

rules.says: A doctor must not solicit patients directly or indirectly, promote services through self-promotion, engage a third party to market medical services, permit use of their name, image, voice, testimonial or endorsement to promote services or products, or join promotional campaigns that give an impression of commercialising practice.
rules.interp: The words “engage any third party for marketing medical services” read broadly, and agencies are a third party. The text on agencies in §4.4 and §8.1(viii) suggests agencies are expected to exist. How these fit is a legal question. See grey areas.

rules.says: A doctor must not give any approval, recommendation, endorsement, certificate, report or statement about any drug, medicine, remedy, therapeutic article, apparatus, appliance, medical device, diagnostic product, health product or commercial product for advertising or publicity linked to their name, signature, photograph, voice or professional status, whether paid or not.
rules.interp: No “doctor recommends” content for skincare brands, devices or supplements, even if unpaid.

rules.says: No celebrity, influencer, patient, employee or third party may be used or permitted to promote professional services through prohibited testimonials, endorsements or recommendations. Any material commercial relationship in lawful public-health or informational communication must be transparently disclosed. A third party must not be used as an intermediary to do indirectly what the doctor or institution may not do directly.
rules.interp: Staff in reels recommending the clinic is an endorsement risk. Influencer collaborations stop unless Leadership and legal counsel clear a purely informational format.

rules.says: Doctors may take part in health awareness programmes, public health campaigns, academic discussions and educational content, provided these do not promote personal practice, do not solicit patients and are not monetised through promotional marketing.
rules.interp: Paid boosting of educational posts to drive appointments could be read as monetising through promotional marketing. See grey areas.

rules.says: Research-based communication, where the doctor has published case studies in reputed medical journals, is allowed as an exception.
rules.interp: Link to the journal publication. Do not turn it into patient-story marketing.

rules.says: A doctor may make a formal announcement about starting practice, change of type of practice, change of address, temporary absence, resuming or succeeding to another practice, and public declaration of consultation fees. Such announcements must be factual, non-promotional and limited in scope.

Doctors may give lectures or talks on public health and diseases for public awareness on TV, radio and electronic media in their own name and designation, without promoting their employer organisation.

Doctors may issue health education and general information pamphlets or brochures to patients visiting their clinic or hospital, without claims of superiority over others, unsubstantiated claims or misleading information.
Doctors may give greetings on days of national importance or related to the medical profession, but without advertising professional gains.
rules.interp: Festival greetings that also carry offers or clinic branding calls to action fall outside this.

rules.says: Campaigns on Government of India or State Government programmes and schemes that are in larger public interest are exempt from the Guidelines.

Hospitals may share factual, objective and verifiable information about their name, location, contact details, departments, facilities, equipment, services, emergency services, accreditation status, charges and other institutional information permitted by law.

Clinical establishments may advertise only factual, objective and verifiable particulars: name, contact details, departments, diagnostic facilities, emergency services, accreditation status, other facilities and applicable fees.
rules.interp: This is the safest model for ad copy: describe what exists, where, and what it costs, in neutral terms.

rules.says: Use of a doctor's photograph is not permitted where it amounts to self-advertisement, solicitation or promotional publicity. Self-photographs or similar publicity material on the letterhead or signboard of a consulting room or clinic are regarded as unethical.
rules.interp: The test is whether the use is promotional. A hero banner with the doctor's face and a booking button looks promotional. A name-and-qualification entry in a factual directory looks informational. We need legal counsel's view (see grey areas).

rules.says: Where advertising is permitted by law, hospital communication must stay within the scope permitted by that law and these Guidelines.
Doctors and clinical establishments should use social media responsibly, balancing public information with patient integrity and professional ethics.

The State Medical Council may contemplate graded action against a doctor: first violation, warning and mandatory ethics training; second, censure and monetary penalty; third, suspension of registration for 3–6 months; serious violation (misleading cure claims, inducement of patients, digital mass solicitation), suspension for 6–12 months; repeated violations, removal from the register for 1–3 years.
rules.interp: These penalties fall on the doctor. This is why clients will be strict and why we should expect faster, firmer approvals from them.

rules.says: Hospitals and institutions engaged in unethical advertising are dealt with under the applicable Clinical Establishments Act and Rules or State Act, including their penalty and appeal routes.
Penalties follow a show-cause notice and a reasoned order. A doctor can appeal to EMRB, NMC within 60 days, and file a second appeal within sixty days of the first decision.
Where a doctor personally authorised, took part in, endorsed or was otherwise responsible for a prohibited communication, their professional conduct may be separately examined.
rules.interp: Keep a record of who approved what, and when, for every client deliverable.
